short_title: People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr.
full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PETITIONER, VS. DATU AKMAD "TATO" AMPATUAN, SR., RESPONDENT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: II. The Revised Penal Code – Book One > B. Criminal Liability > 7. Participation in Acts Giving Rise to Criminal Liability > b. Conspiracy and Proposal > i. As a Mode of Incurring Criminal Liability
topics: Overt act in furtherance of a conspiracy vs. mere approval or acquiescence
Liability of a conspirator absent from the crime scene; moral ascendancy must be proved
Finality-of-acquittal rule; certiorari against an acquittal only for grave abuse of discretion
Gross misapprehension of facts as grave abuse: must also be capricious or whimsical

doctrine:
**To be liable as a conspirator, the accused must have performed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy, that is, an act that promotes, advances, or facilitates the progress of the plan.** The overt act may be active participation in the crime itself, or moral assistance by being present at its commission or by exerting moral ascendancy over the co-conspirators. **Mere presence at the planning, and statements made in agreement with the plot, are approval or acquiescence, not acts in furtherance, and are not enough to convict**, unless the approval is so indispensable that without it the plan would not be set in motion or carried out. By contrast, offering one's guns for the killing is an overt act even if other guns were used: the act need only be done *in furtherance* of the conspiracy; it need not actually further it. A conspirator absent from the scene is liable only if it is proved that his moral ascendancy moved the others to carry out the plan. Moral ascendancy cannot be presumed from kinship or public position.

**A judgment of acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory** (finality-of-acquittal rule, which shares the purpose of the right against double jeopardy). It may be challenged only by certiorari for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, as where the prosecution was denied the opportunity to present its case or the trial was a sham. Gross misapprehension of facts is not by itself an exception to double jeopardy. It establishes grave abuse only if it is patent and gross and was exercised in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner, because "[w]himsicality, not accuracy, is the core of certiorari proceedings."

Under **Article 20 of the RPC**, one who would otherwise be an accessory is exempt when the principal is a relative within the degrees stated, including relatives by affinity within the same degrees (here, the son-in-law of a principal).
facts:
Datu Akmad "Tato" Ampatuan, Sr., then OIC Vice Governor of Maguindanao and the nephew and son-in-law of clan patriarch Datu Andal Ampatuan, Sr., was charged with 58 counts of murder over the November 23, 2009 Maguindanao massacre. He attended the clan meetings where the plot to kill Datu Esmael "Toto" Mangudadatu was discussed: at Century Park Hotel on July 20, 2009, and on November 17 and 22, 2009. At one meeting he said "Pakinggan natin si Ama. Okay kami lahat na patayin sila" and "mabuti nga sa mga Mangudadatu na mahilig mag-ambisyon na patayin sila lahat." No eyewitness placed him at the crime site. He attended a medical mission the whole day of November 23, 2009.

In its December 19, 2019 Consolidated Partial Decision, the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 221, convicted several Ampatuans of 57 counts of murder. Among them was Datu Zaldy Ampatuan, who was absent from the scene but had pledged at a meeting: "Todo suporta ako diyan, kahit lahat ng baril ko gagamitin ko." The RTC acquitted Datu Akmad on reasonable doubt. It classed him among those who had prior knowledge of the plot but performed no overt act.

The State, through the OSG, filed a Rule 65 petition for certiorari with the CA. The CA dismissed it (Decision of May 24, 2021; Resolution of December 10, 2021), holding that the alleged errors went to the merits, that double jeopardy had attached, and that mere presence at meetings and acquiescence, without an overt act, did not make him a conspirator. The State then filed a Rule 45 petition. It argued that he expressed conformity with and encouraged the plan; that his situation was like that of Datu Zaldy and Datu Anwar, who were convicted though absent; that he lent his man Talembo "Tammy" Masukat, who joined the killing; that his absence was part of the plan, with absent clan members on standby to monitor and assist; and that at the least he was an accessory. Datu Akmad invoked the lack of an overt act, Article 20 of the RPC, and double jeopardy.
issues: Whether the CA correctly held that the RTC did not commit grave abuse of discretion in acquitting Datu Akmad, given the finality-of-acquittal rule and the right against double jeopardy.
Whether Datu Akmad's attendance at the planning meetings, his statements of approval, and his relationship with Talembo constitute overt acts in furtherance of the conspiracy.
Whether Datu Akmad may be held liable as an accessory.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the CA correctly found no grave abuse of discretion.** An acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory. It may be challenged without violating double jeopardy only for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, such as denial of the prosecution's chance to present its case or a sham trial. Gross misapprehension of facts may be used to show grave abuse but is not per se an exception. It must be patent and gross and also committed in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner. **Errors of judgment, misapplication of facts, and erroneous conclusions cannot be reviewed without trampling on the right against double jeopardy.** On a Rule 45 review of a CA ruling in a Rule 65 case, the Court asks only whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse, not whether the RTC decided the case correctly on the merits.

**2. No overt act was proved.** Quoting Bahilidad v. People, the Court held that a conspirator must have performed some overt act as a direct or indirect contribution to the crime, and that mere presence at the discussion of a conspiracy, "even approval of it, without any active participation," is not enough. Using Black's definitions, an overt act is an outward act done *in furtherance* of the conspiracy, and furtherance means facilitating the plan's progress or making it more likely to occur.

- *Datu Zaldy vs. Datu Akmad:* Datu Zaldy's offer of all his guns was an overt act, because the guns were the very tools needed for the killing. It counted even if other guns were used, since the act need only be "in furtherance of a conspiracy, not that it furthers the conspiracy." **Datu Akmad's statements, "debauched and depraved as they may be, are mere expressions of approval of or acquiescence to the plot."** Evidence of actual cooperation is required, not mere cognizance or approval. His approval was not indispensable, because the plan would have been carried out without it.
- *Moral ascendancy:* An absent conspirator may be liable if, through moral ascendancy, he moved the others to execute the plan. Apart from his being the patriarch's nephew and OIC Vice Governor, there was no proof that he exerted such ascendancy, and the RTC was silent on the effect of his words. **"Courts cannot rely on mere presumptions of moral ascendancy."**
- *Monitoring and standby:* The plan for others to monitor and help came from Datu Unsay. Datu Akmad's awareness of that statement was not agreement to it, much less an overt act.
- *Talembo:* There was no evidence that Datu Akmad offered Talembo's services. Talembo was a CVO commander who took directives from several bosses, including Datu Unsay, and the petition itself admitted only a "possibility." The Court would not rely on speculation.
- *Medical mission:* Even if the RTC erred in finding that he did not "cling" to the plot, "clinging" is not itself an overt act. It means only adherence or acquiescence, which is insufficient to convict.

**3. No accessory liability.** Even assuming he could be deemed an accessory, he is the son-in-law of principal accused Datu Andal, Sr. **Article 20 of the RPC exempts him**, because accessories are not penalized when the principal is their relative by affinity within the same degrees. The Court stressed that this "by no means signifies his innocence"; the law recognizes that family ties compel one to conceal crimes of near relatives.
disposition: The Petition was DENIED. The CA's May 24, 2021 Decision and December 10, 2021 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 164524, which dismissed the State's petition for certiorari, stand. Datu Akmad's acquittal was therefore left undisturbed.

bar_questions.q: Brothers Ariel and Benny met at their father's house with their cousin Cesar to plan the killing of a political rival. Ariel laid out the plan. Cesar, who sat through the whole meeting, said: "Tama, dapat lang siyang patayin." On the day of the killing, Ariel and Benny ambushed and killed the rival. Cesar was at a wedding in another town. No evidence showed that Cesar gave any money, weapon, men, or instructions, or that his words influenced the brothers. Is Cesar liable for murder as a conspirator?

alac.answer: No. Cesar is not liable as a conspirator because he performed no overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy.
alac.legal_basis: A conspirator must perform an overt act, an act that promotes, advances, or facilitates the progress of the conspiratorial plan, as a direct or indirect contribution to the crime. It may be active participation in the crime, or moral assistance through presence at its commission or moral ascendancy over the co-conspirators. Mere presence at the discussion of a conspiracy, and even approval of it, without active participation, is not enough to convict. Statements made in agreement with the plot must be distinguished from statements made in furtherance of it. (People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr., G.R. No. 258710, January 27, 2025, citing Bahilidad v. People)
alac.application: Cesar's attendance at the meeting and his remark that the rival deserved to die are expressions of approval or acquiescence, like Datu Akmad's statements in Ampatuan. They did not promote or facilitate the plan. His approval was not indispensable, since Ariel and Benny carried out the killing on their own. He was not present at the crime, and there is no proof that he had moral ascendancy over the brothers or that his words moved them to act.
alac.conclusion: Cesar must be acquitted because mere approval of the plot, without an overt act in furtherance of it, does not make him a conspirator.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as in the previous problem, except that at the planning meeting their uncle Dado, who was also absent from the ambush, declared: "Full support ako. Gamitin ninyo lahat ng baril ko para malinis ang trabaho." In the end, Ariel and Benny used their own guns. The prosecution also argues that Cesar, as the provincial vice governor and the eldest cousin, must have had moral ascendancy over the brothers. (a) Is Dado liable as a conspirator? (b) Does the prosecution's argument make Cesar liable?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Dado committed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy by offering his guns, even though they were not used. (b) No. Moral ascendancy must be proved and cannot be presumed from Cesar's position or relationship.
alac.legal_basis: An overt act need only be done in furtherance of the conspiracy; it need not actually further it. In People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr. (G.R. No. 258710, January 27, 2025), the Court held that Datu Zaldy's offer of "lahat ng baril ko" was an overt act showing unity of design, because guns are the very tools of the killing, even if other guns were later used. A conspirator remote from the scene may be liable if it is proved that his moral ascendancy moved the others to carry out the plan. But "[c]ourts cannot rely on mere presumptions of moral ascendancy," and being a relative and a vice governor is not proof of it.
alac.application: (a) Dado did more than approve the plan: he offered the means to execute it. That offer advanced the plan and showed his unity of purpose with the brothers, so his absence from the scene and the brothers' use of other guns do not matter. (b) The prosecution offers only Cesar's office and his seniority in the family. Nothing shows that his words produced any reaction or that the brothers acted because of him. Moral ascendancy cannot be inferred from status alone.
alac.conclusion: Dado is liable as a conspirator, but Cesar is not, because moral ascendancy over the brothers was not proved.

bar_questions.q: After trial, the RTC acquitted Ramon of murder, finding that the prosecution had failed to prove an overt act on his part. The prosecution, which had presented all its witnesses and evidence, filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 65 with the CA. It argued that the RTC misappreciated the testimony of its witnesses and drew wrong conclusions from them. The prosecution also argued that Ramon, who knew of the plan and later helped hide his father-in-law (a principal) from the police, should at least be convicted as an accessory. (a) Will the certiorari petition prosper? (b) Can Ramon be held liable as an accessory?

alac.answer: (a) No. The petition will not prosper because it raises only errors of judgment, and reviewing them would violate the right against double jeopardy. (b) No. Ramon is exempt as an accessory under Article 20 of the RPC because the principal is his father-in-law.
alac.legal_basis: A judgment of acquittal is final, unappealable, and immediately executory. It may be assailed through certiorari only for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, as where the prosecution was denied the opportunity to present its case or the trial was a sham. Misappreciation of evidence and erroneous conclusions are errors of judgment. Even gross misapprehension of facts amounts to grave abuse only if exercised in a capricious, arbitrary, whimsical, or despotic manner: "[w]himsicality, not accuracy, is the core of certiorari proceedings." Under Article 20 of the RPC, the penalties for accessories are not imposed on those who are such with respect to their spouses, ascendants, descendants, legitimate, natural, and adopted brothers and sisters, or relatives by affinity within the same degrees, except accessories under paragraph 1 of Article 19. (People v. Datu Akmad Ampatuan, Sr., G.R. No. 258710, January 27, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The prosecution was fully heard, and it claims only that the RTC weighed the evidence wrongly. That is an error of judgment, not a capricious or whimsical exercise of discretion that ousted the RTC of jurisdiction. Reviewing the acquittal would place Ramon twice in jeopardy. (b) Helping conceal his father-in-law from the police falls under paragraph 3 of Article 19 (harboring or concealing the principal), not paragraph 1 (profiting from the crime). Since the principal is his relative by affinity in the direct line, Article 20 exempts him. As the Court noted, the exemption does not mean he is innocent; the law recognizes that family ties compel concealment of near relatives' crimes.
alac.conclusion: The certiorari petition will be dismissed, and Ramon cannot be penalized as an accessory.

notes: The Court cited an earlier ruling involving the same respondent, Datu Akmad "Tato" Ampatuan, Sr. v. Hon. Secretary of Justice, G.R. No. 200106, February 22, 2023, for the observation that his acquittal rested on the prosecution's failure to prove an overt act. Bar question 3(b) relies on the paragraph 1 exception quoted in Article 20 and on the basic text of Article 19 (paragraph 3 covers harboring or concealing the principal); the decision itself applied only Article 20.
